children: is expanding its global manufacturing footprint with a new $2.75 billion semiconductor assembly and test facility in Gujarat, India, as demand for memory and storage continues to accelerate alongside artificial intelligence. CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said Micron plans to scale production at the Sanand facility next year, giving the company additional capacity as AI workloads drive heavier demand for DRAM and NAND products.
The facility represents a combined investment of roughly $2.75 billion from Micron and its government partners.
Micron has already begun commercial production at Sanand, with finished DRAM and NAND products now being shipped to customers globally.

"For decades, people have talked about India's semiconductor potential. I have been in many of those conversations. Potential does not ship products. What I see in India today is execution," Mehrotra said at SEMICON India 2026.
He added that production capacity at the facility already exceeds the amount of memory required for India's entire laptop market.

"Earlier this year, we began commercial production at Sanand, Gujarat. It is the first semiconductor assembly and test facility here in India and the first project under the India semiconductor mission...finished DRAM and NAND products are now leaving Gujarat for customers around the world carrying a label this country has waited a long time to put on a memory chip - the Made in India," Mehrotra said.
The India expansion focuses on conventional assembly and testing while complementing Micron's planned investments in more advanced manufacturing and packaging capacity in the United States.
The Sanand facility gives Micron another lever for expanding output without concentrating all future capacity in one geography.
More importantly, the timing aligns with unusually strong memory demand driven by AI infrastructure.
Investors should watch how quickly the facility ramps, whether higher capacity supports shipment growth and how additional supply affects pricing across DRAM and NAND.
The bullish case is straightforward: if AI demand remains strong, Micron can use added capacity to capture more volume while strengthening its global supply chain.

The risk is that memory remains cyclical. Expanding capacity aggressively into a strong pricing environment can become problematic if industry supply eventually grows faster than demand. For now, however, Micron is positioning Sanand as another piece of the infrastructure needed to support the next phase of memory growth.

title: Micron Sends Fresh Signal to AI Chip Investors
